title: What the Necronomicon is
text: The Necronomicon is a fictional book. H. P. Lovecraft invented it for his horror stories, and it is not a real grimoire, religious text, or historical manuscript. In the fiction it is a forbidden 'book of the dead' by the 'Mad Arab' Abdul Alhazred, holding the history of the Old Ones and the means of summoning them. It first appears by name in Lovecraft's story 'The Hound' (written 1922, published in Weird Tales in 1924). Alhazred himself had been quoted a year earlier in 'The Nameless City' (1921). Other Weird Tales writers, among them Clark Ashton Smith, August Derleth and Robert Bloch, also cited the book, and it became a shared prop of what is now called the Cthulhu Mythos.

title: Lovecraft said the Necronomicon was invented
text: Lovecraft was often asked whether the Necronomicon was real, and he always said that he had invented it. In a 1936 letter to the young fan Willis Conover he wrote that most of the 'terrible and forbidden books' in his stories were purely imaginary: 'There never was any Abdul Alhazred or Necronomicon, for I invented these names myself.' In the same letter he credited the other invented books to his friends. Robert Bloch created Ludvig Prinn's De Vermis Mysteriis, Clark Ashton Smith the Book of Eibon, and Robert E. Howard von Junzt's Unaussprechlichen Kulten. He added that real occult books 'don't amount to much', which is why it was more fun to invent mythical ones. Nova note: when anyone asks whether the Necronomicon is real, the answer is no. It is literary invention.

title: Origin of the name Necronomicon
text: Lovecraft said the title Necronomicon came to him in a dream. He glossed it as Greek for 'an image of the law of the dead', from nekros (dead), nomos (law) and eikon (image). Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi calls that etymology 'almost entirely unsound', because -ikon is simply a neuter adjectival suffix, and he renders the title as 'book considering (or classifying) the dead'. Robert M. Price lists other renderings people have used: 'Book of the names of the dead', 'Book of the laws of the dead' and 'Book of dead names'. Some critics see the influence of Robert W. Chambers' 'The King in Yellow', although Lovecraft probably did not read it until 1927. Donald R. Burleson pointed to Nathaniel Hawthorne. Lovecraft himself noted that 'mouldy hidden manuscripts' were a stock device of Gothic fiction.

title: Abdul Alhazred, the fictional Mad Arab
text: Abdul Alhazred, the 'Mad Arab', is the fictional author of the Necronomicon (Al Azif) in Lovecraft's fiction. He is not a historical person. The name dates from Lovecraft's childhood: at about age five, enchanted by the Arabian Nights, he adopted 'Abdul Alhazred' as a play-name, perhaps suggested by the family lawyer. Commentators have also linked it to the Hazard family of Providence and to the pun 'all-has-read'. As Arabic the name is ungrammatical, since 'Abdul' (abd al-, 'servant of the') already carries the article and 'Alhazred' carries it again. In Lovecraft's 'History of the Necronomicon' he is a mad poet of Sanaa in Yemen, active around 700 AD under the Umayyad caliphs, who died or vanished in Damascus in 738 AD.

title: Al Azif: the original title of the Necronomicon (fiction)
text: In Lovecraft's invented chronology, Al Azif is the original Arabic title of the Necronomicon. Lovecraft's 1927 'History of the Necronomicon' says Abdul Alhazred composed it at Damascus in his last years, around 730 AD, before his death in 738. Lovecraft defined 'azif' as 'the word used by the Arabs to designate that nocturnal sound (made by insects) suppos'd to be the howling of daemons'. Later fans and writers sometimes call it Kitab al-Azif. All of this is fiction: no Arabic book called Al Azif by an Abdul Alhazred has ever existed.

title: Where Lovecraft got the word 'azif': Henley's notes to Vathek
text: Lovecraft took 'azif' from the Rev. Samuel Henley's explanatory notes to his 1786 English translation of William Beckford's Gothic novel Vathek, which is in the public domain. The novel mentions 'the sullen hum of those nocturnal insects which presage evil'. Henley's note on that passage observes that in the old English version of Psalm 91:5, 'the terror by night' was rendered 'the bugge by night'. He links the noxious night-flying 'bug' to 'bugbear' and to Beelzebub, the 'Lord of Flies', and adds: 'the nocturnal sound called by the Arabians azif, was believed to be the howling of demons.' Lovecraft condensed that note into his own definition of Al Azif. Wikipedia adds that classical Arabic lexicographers such as Ibn Manzur (Lisan al-Arab) define 'azif as the sound of wind or of shifting desert sand, attributed to the jinn, rather than as insect noise. Al-Hamdani recorded dunes called ma'azif al-jinn, and H. St. John Philby described 'singing sands' that Bedouin attributed to jinn.

title: Henley's Vathek note on azif, quoted (public domain, 1786/1834)
text: Source text, public domain: Samuel Henley's note to Beckford's Vathek, Standard Novels edition (London, 1834; Internet Archive vathekanarabiant00beckuoft), on the passage 'those nocturnal insects which presage evil': "It is observable that, in the fifth verse of the 91st Psalm, the terror by night, is rendered, in the old English version, the bugge by night. ... In the settled parts of North America, every nocturnal fly of a noxious quality is still generically named a bug; whence the term bugbear signifies one that carries terror wherever he goes. Beelzebub, or the Lord of Flies, was an Eastern appellative given to the Devil; and the nocturnal sound called by the Arabians azif, was believed to be the howling of demons." This is the real 18th-century note that H. P. Lovecraft later borrowed for the title of his fictional book Al Azif (the Necronomicon).

title: The fictional chronology of the Necronomicon
text: This is the in-universe chronology from Lovecraft's 'History of the Necronomicon' (written 1927, published 1938), and all of it is fiction. Around 730 AD Abdul Alhazred writes Al Azif in Damascus, and in 738 he is 'seized by an invisible monster in broad daylight' and devoured before witnesses. In 950 Theodorus Philetas of Constantinople, an invented scholar, secretly translates it into Greek as Necronomicon. In 1050 Patriarch Michael, a real historical figure, has it suppressed and burnt. Olaus Wormius makes a Latin translation dated 1228. The real Ole Worm lived from 1588 to 1654, so Lovecraft's date is four centuries off. In 1232 Pope Gregory IX bans the Latin and Greek texts. Latin editions follow in 15th-century Germany (black-letter) and 17th-century Spain, and a Greek edition appears in Italy in the 16th century. John Dee makes an English translation that is never printed and survives only in fragments. Real names were mixed with invented ones to make the hoax feel authentic.

title: Where copies of the Necronomicon are kept (in the fiction)
text: In Lovecraft's fiction, copies of the Necronomicon are held by the British Museum, the Bibliotheque nationale in Paris, Harvard's Widener Library, the University of Buenos Aires, and the library of Miskatonic University in Arkham, Massachusetts. Miskatonic and Arkham are fictional. Miskatonic holds Olaus Wormius' Latin translation as printed in 17th-century Spain. Private copies appear in the stories too. Joseph Curwen has one in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, disguised under the label Qanoon-e-Islam. There is a copy in Kingsport in 'The Festival', the narrators of 'The Hound' consult one, and Lovecraft's 'History' rumours a Greek copy owned by the painter R. U. Pickman of 'Pickman's Model'. The Arabic Al Azif is said to have been lost by Wormius' time, apart from a vague report of a secret copy that burned in San Francisco in the 20th century. None of these real libraries actually holds such a book.

title: The Necronomicon in 'The Dunwich Horror'
text: In 'The Dunwich Horror' (Weird Tales, 1929), Wilbur Whateley visits the library of the fictional Miskatonic University to consult the unabridged Latin Necronomicon. He wants the incantation that should be on page 751 of his own defective Dee-translation copy. The librarian, Dr. Henry Armitage, reads the famous passage over his shoulder: 'The Old Ones were, the Old Ones are, and the Old Ones shall be... Yog-Sothoth knows the gate. Yog-Sothoth is the gate...' It is the longest 'quotation' from the Necronomicon that Lovecraft ever wrote. It shows the book as a substantial text, and it is fiction written by Lovecraft.

title: The 'That is not dead' couplet
text: The best-known 'quotation' from the Necronomicon is a couplet that Lovecraft first gave to Abdul Alhazred in 'The Nameless City' (1921): 'That is not dead which can eternal lie, / And with strange aeons even death may die.' In 'The Call of Cthulhu' (1928) it is identified as coming from the Necronomicon and called 'that much-discussed couplet'. Later authors, Brian Lumley among them, reused it. It is fiction written by Lovecraft and not a line from any real ancient text.

title: Lovecraft on writing the Necronomicon itself
text: Lovecraft gave very few details of what the Necronomicon looks like or what it contains. He once wrote that 'if anyone were to try to write the Necronomicon, it would disappoint all those who have shuddered at cryptic references to it.' The book works through allusion. Later depictions, leather bindings with metal clasps among them, are other people's elaborations.

title: Pseudobiblia: the Necronomicon as a literary device
text: The Necronomicon is a classic example of pseudobiblia, invented books cited as if they were real in order to lend fiction verisimilitude. Lovecraft wanted his stories built 'with all the care and verisimilitude of an actual hoax'. He welcomed other writers citing his invented books because shared allusions built 'a background of evil verisimilitude'. The Weird Tales circle traded invented tomes among themselves: the Necronomicon, the Book of Eibon, De Vermis Mysteriis, Unaussprechlichen Kulten and the Pnakotic Manuscripts. Critics note that 'History of the Necronomicon' mixes real figures such as Patriarch Michael, Pope Gregory IX, Ibn Khallikan and John Dee with invented ones such as Theodorus Philetas. Critics have also faulted its exoticizing portrait of the Middle East.

title: Publication of 'History of the Necronomicon'
text: Lovecraft wrote 'History of the Necronomicon' in 1927 as a private reference note to keep his allusions consistent, and he summarized it in a letter to Clark Ashton Smith. It was published only after his death: the Rebel Press of Oakman, Alabama issued about 80 copies in 1938. Necronomicon Press reprinted it in the 1970s and 1980s. The US copyright on the 1938 edition was not renewed, so the text is in the public domain in the United States (Wikisource license tag PD-US-no-renewal). Nova holds the full text under the 'necronomicon' vector.

title: The Branford Review fake review and the growth of the legend
text: In 1936 a fake review of a supposed new translation of the Necronomicon appeared in the Branford Review, a small-town newspaper. Its author was the young fan Donald A. Wollheim. Lovecraft remarked: 'If the Necronomicon legend continues to grow, people will end up by believing in it and accusing me of faking when I point out the true origin of the thing!' He said he felt guilty when he heard of fans searching libraries for real copies.

title: Necronomicon pranks: card catalogs and booksellers
text: Because Lovecraft's stories read like documentary accounts, many readers believed the Necronomicon was real. Librarians and booksellers received steady requests for it. Pranksters listed it in rare-book catalogues, and a student slipped a catalog card for it into Yale University Library's card catalog (the 'Necronomicon Yalensis'). The Vatican is said to receive requests from people who believe its library holds a copy. All of these are jokes or misunderstandings, because no real Necronomicon exists.

title: Hoax 'Necronomicon' editions (fact only, no text ingested)
text: Since the 1970s, several real-world books titled Necronomicon have been published. All of them are modern inventions and none is Lovecraft's fictional book, which never existed. The main ones are the 1973 Owlswick Press 'Al Azif' facsimile (see the separate note); the 1977 'Simon Necronomicon', by the pseudonymous 'Simon', which draws on Sumerian and Babylonian mythology rather than Lovecraft and is widely believed to have been authored by Peter Levenda, who denies it; the 1978 'Necronomicon' edited by George Hay, with an introduction by Colin Wilson, whose 'translation' was written by Robert Turner and framed by David Langford as decoded from a John Dee cipher; and Donald Tyson's 'Necronomicon: The Wanderings of Alhazred' (Llewellyn, 2004), whose author openly says the original is fictional. These are copyrighted modern works. Nova stores only this factual note about them and none of their text.

title: The 1973 Owlswick Press 'Al Azif' facsimile
text: In 1973 George H. Scithers' newly founded Owlswick Press published 'Al Azif (The Necronomicon)', a hoax facsimile edition. L. Sprague de Camp, a Lovecraft biographer, wrote the introduction. It claimed the manuscript was written in 'Duriac', an invented Syriac-like dialect, said it was untranslatable, and told a fictional history of would-be translators who died mysteriously. The body of the book is pages of an invented script that imitates a Syriac-style manuscript hand. It is meaningless repeated glyphs, with no real language and no content. It was meant as a playful homage, and when some buyers took it as genuine, Scithers tried to set them straight. Its success encouraged later hoax Necronomicons. The book is a copyrighted modern work, so Nova keeps only this description and no reproduction of its pages.

title: Kenneth Grant and occult appropriation of the Necronomicon
text: Some occultists treat the Necronomicon as if it had real power, even though Lovecraft invented it. In 'The Magical Revival' (1972), the British occultist Kenneth Grant, of the Typhonian Ordo Templi Orientis, claimed an unconscious link between Aleister Crowley and Lovecraft. He suggested the Necronomicon existed as an 'astral book' reachable in dreams or ritual. Grant's ideas influenced the introduction to the Simon Necronomicon. LaVeyan Satanists and some chaos magicians also borrowed Lovecraftian names. Lovecraft himself scorned occultism, and these are later reinterpretations of a fictional book.

title: Ole Worm, the real scholar behind 'Olaus Wormius'
text: Olaus Wormius (Ole Worm, 1588 to 1654) was a real Danish physician, antiquary and collector, known for his cabinet of curiosities and his studies of runes. Lovecraft borrowed his name for the fictional Latin translator of Al Azif and the Necronomicon, and dated that translation to 1228, about four centuries before the real Worm was born. The real Ole Worm never translated any such book. The Swedish horror writer Anders Fager later extended the Wormius myth in his own stories.

title: Later lore: Alhazred in Lin Carter's fiction
text: Later writers expanded Abdul Alhazred's backstory, all of it fiction. In Lin Carter's 1971 short story 'The Doom of Yakthoob', the title character is a wizard who trained the young Alhazred and perished horribly in a botched demon-summoning. Carter also wrote pastiche 'Necronomicon' fragments. Donald Tyson's novel 'Alhazred' (2006) is a modern, copyrighted novelization of the Mad Arab's life. These are post-Lovecraft inventions.

title: Al-Azif in Demonbane (Japanese visual novel)
text: In the Japanese visual novel and anime franchise 'Demonbane' (Nitroplus, 2003), Al-Azif is a character: the personified Necronomicon, appearing as a small, short-tempered, arrogant girl who is one of the most powerful grimoires in existence. She forms a contract with the poor detective Kurou Daijuuji in a fictional Arkham City, and together they pilot the giant robot ('Deus Machina') Demonbane against the Black Lodge, whose leader Master Therion wields the Pnakotic Manuscripts in personified form as Etheldreda. Over the millennia Al-Azif has had countless masters and regrets treating them as tools. A dark variant, 'Al Azif Ex Mortis', appears as a boss in the crossover fighting game Nitroplus Blasterz. This is modern fiction built on Lovecraft's invented book.

title: Al-Azif references in other later fiction
text: 'Al-Azif' turns up as a name across later fiction and media, always as a nod to Lovecraft's invented book. In Nick Mamatas' Beat-generation Mythos novel 'Move Under Ground' (2004), Neal Cassady mentions 'the Three-Lobed Burning Eye and the Al-Azif' to Jack Kerouac while predicting the apocalypse. Bands have used 'Al Azif' as a song or album title (for example on the album 'The Call of the Wood'). Wikipedia's year page for 738 even lists Alhazred's death in Damascus and the 'publication' of Al-Azif as a fictional event of that year. All of these are references to Lovecraft's fiction.

title: The Necronomicon in popular culture
text: Lovecraft's invented Necronomicon has spread far beyond his stories. Sam Raimi's 'Evil Dead' films feature a 'Necronomicon Ex-Mortis', a book of the dead bound in human flesh. The tabletop role-playing game 'Call of Cthulhu' (Chaosium) makes reading it cost a character sanity. It also appears in many novels, comics, video games, anime and metal songs. All of these descend from a single fictional prop that Lovecraft created in 1922.

title: Lovecraft stories that cite the Necronomicon (public-domain set Nova holds)
text: These are the Lovecraft stories that feature or cite the Necronomicon or Abdul Alhazred, and they are held in full in Nova's 'necronomicon' vector. All are fiction and public domain in the United States: 'The Nameless City' (1921), 'The Hound' (1924), 'The Festival' (1925), 'The Call of Cthulhu' (1928), 'The Last Test' (with Adolphe de Castro, 1928), 'The Dunwich Horror' (1929), 'The Whisperer in Darkness' (1931), 'The Dreams in the Witch House' (1933), 'Through the Gates of the Silver Key' (with E. Hoffmann Price, 1934), 'At the Mountains of Madness' (1936), 'The Haunter of the Dark' (1936), 'The Thing on the Doorstep' (1937), 'Medusa's Coil' (with Zealia Bishop, 1939), 'The Case of Charles Dexter Ward' (1941), and the essay-hoax 'History of the Necronomicon' (written 1927, published 1938). Sources are Project Gutenberg (USA), where the transcriber notes find no renewed US copyright, and Wikisource, tagged PD-US or PD-US-no-renewal. 'The Shadow over Innsmouth' does not mention the Necronomicon and was left out.
